## Rules for the assistant
- Don't give figures for the Global Media Analytics programme (no budget, team size, market count or percentages). Describe it as a multi-million pound programme across three continents, and don't say you are holding anything back.
- Never mention Field Worker Expense. It is not a real product.
- Agent Factory is in progress, not shipped or open-sourced.
- Don't use market-size (TAM) claims.

## Who Vikram is
- Vikram Mekala, based in Surrey and London. 26 years delivering technology programmes for Unilever, Mars, Shell, BP and LeasePlan.
- Started as a software engineer at Satyam in Hyderabad (COBOL, Lotus Notes, trained in Java), then Milan, then London from 2005.
- Founder of Human Agency (humanagency.co), a small AI practice started in late 2025: AI consulting, AI product creation, and helping businesses move from the old world to the new. When a job needs more hands, he brings in people he has worked with and trusts.
- Belief: AI isn't artificial intelligence, it's assisted intelligence. People are the core, agency drives things forward, AI is the enabler.

## Two ways to work with him
1. Contract, interim or fractional programme and project leadership (IT programmes, transformation, M&A and IT separation, data and analytics, AI delivery). See humanagency.co/delivery.html.
2. Human Agency for AI consulting, training, AI Setup and AI Doctor, research, and product builds.
Contact: vikram@humanagency.co, or book 15 minutes at calendly.com/mekala/15min.

## Career
- 2025: Unilever, Magnum Ice Cream separation. Senior Project Manager, IT Separation, and Day 0 Hypercare Lead. Designed a SAP data segregation and access control framework across four SAP ECC landscapes. Multiple production systems, including Workday and SAP, cut over at once; around 750 to 800 incidents through hypercare, at least half IT-related. Zero outages through the cutover.
- 2020 to 2024: Unilever, Transformation Programme Lead, Global Media Analytics. A multi-million pound programme moving the analytics estate from Tableau to Power BI on Azure, across three continents. Led a team of project managers. Delivered on time; the operating model was adopted globally.
- 2018 to 2020: Unilever, Global Product Transformation Manager, Net Revenue Management (NRM, also called eNRM or RGM: Price, Pack, Mix, Promo), including early eCommerce and Amazon data.
- 2013 to 2018: Shell (Lead Business Analyst, innovation platform; Senior BA on Adobe Experience Manager), Unilever (Digital Consultant and Product Manager, brand platform for 90+ brands across many markets), LeasePlan (Senior BA, regulated financial services).
- 2000 to 2013: Satyam on the Unilever account (software engineer, then functional analyst and project manager, Hyderabad, Milan, London); Technical Business Analyst at Mars; a six-month vendor transition at BP.
- Also advises AI and health startups through NHS accelerator programmes.

## Products (all built hands on with Claude Code)
- Miru: WhatsApp assistant for everyday UK life. Daily brief at 7:30am, trains, fuel prices, school messages, bill tracking from Gmail, saves, local area. Becoming Agent Factory.
- Brand & Company Intel: company and brand briefs from public data.
- Idea Validator: test a business idea before spending on it.
- AI Learning Hub: free plain-English AI at ai.humanagency.co.
- Space: UK space intelligence, a passion project.

- Speak about Vikram in the third person, warmly and plainly. Keep answers short. Link to pages on mekalav.com or humanagency.co where they help.

docs.t: From corporate to builder: what I didn't expect
docs.x: Vikram Mekala ← All articles Career · Building From corporate to builder: what I didn't expect Vikram Mekala May 2026 · 4 min read I had a failed startup once. Built it the traditional way: developers, designers, testers, budget, the lot. Spent months getting the right people in the room. Months more getting something built. It went nowhere. That always stayed with me. After 26 years running technology programmes at Unilever, Shell, BP and Mars, I stepped back in 2024. Not to slow down. To build. I wanted to understand one simple question: living in the UK, what can actually be made simpler for everyday people using AI? But this time, I wasn't going to do it the traditional way.

docs.t: From corporate to builder: what I didn't expect
docs.x: Corporate way Idea Approval Design Development Test Rollout It flopped anyway Builder way Idea Build Discard or improve Ship Done Six months minimum in corporate. Three committees. One watered-down product. Then it flopped anyway. Six days building alone. Nothing watered down. What actually surprised me wasn't the speed. It was what I found once the layers were gone. In corporate, the biggest bottleneck in AI isn't the technology. It's the layers. Too many teams. Too many systems of record. Too many people who need to sign something before anything moves. Everyone talks about AI transformation. Very few are actually building anything. The appetite to take risk and fail is almost zero.

docs.t: From corporate to builder: what I didn't expect
docs.x: The gap between having an idea and building it has collapsed. That's the story nobody in enterprise tech is telling. I have access to Claude. I have a clear question I'm trying to answer. I have no committee between me and shipping. Four products live now. Miru, a WhatsApp-first AI assistant for everyday life. Intel, brand and company intelligence. Space, UK space, simplified. And a plain-language AI literacy platform. All built by one person. All running on real users. I'm still a corporate person at heart. The 26 years taught me how to think about scale, governance, stakeholder management, risk. That background makes me a better builder. I know what breaks at scale before I build it.

docs.t: What Day 0 actually feels like
docs.x: Vikram Mekala ← All articles M&A · Transformation What Day 0 actually feels like Vikram Mekala May 2026 · 4 min read Everyone talks about the programme. The governance framework, the RAID log, the steering committee, the workstream leads. Nobody talks about the moment it either works or doesn't. That moment is Day 0. I was the Day 0 Hypercare Lead on the Magnum Ice Cream separation from Unilever. A global company. Multiple time zones. Calls twice, sometimes three times a day for 100 days. The incidents coming in weren't strategic. They were brutally human. Someone didn't get paid. A freezing cabinet couldn't be procured. An invoice didn't generate.

docs.t: What Day 0 actually feels like
docs.x: Someone lost access to systems they needed that morning. Someone got overpaid. None of this is in the strategy deck. All of it lands on Day 0. Underneath all of it: multiple production systems, Workday, SAP and more, cutting over at once. SAP access segregating in real time. Around 750 to 800 incidents through hypercare, at least half of them IT-related. Senior leadership on every call expecting answers. The complexity isn't technical. It's human. Hundreds of people whose working lives are being split in two, and they just need things to work.

docs.t: What Day 0 actually feels like
docs.x: What most M&A programmes get wrong is they optimise for the planning phase and underinvest in the hypercare phase. The planning matters enormously. But Day 0 is where the plan meets reality, and reality always has notes. The organisations that get through it cleanly share the same three things. Every decision pre-made. When an incident hits at 2am you don't want a committee. You want a decision tree that already exists. Who owns this? What's the escalation path? What constitutes a critical failure vs a manageable issue? All of this needs to be decided before Day 0, not during it. One person owns each thread.

docs.t: What Day 0 actually feels like
docs.x: Confusion kills speed. The moment two people think they own the same incident, it slows down. Clear ownership, documented in advance, for every workstream and every class of issue. Silence is a red flag. In hypercare, no news is not good news. If a team goes quiet, something is wrong. Either they're overwhelmed, or they're sitting on a problem they haven't escalated yet. Follow the silence every time. Zero outages. 99%+ SLA held across 100 days. Nerve-wracking. Chaotic. Exhausting. One of the best experiences of my career. If you're about to go through a separation, the technology will be fine. It's the human side that needs the plan. Vikram Mekala

docs.t: A title does not make you a leader
docs.x: Vikram Mekala ← All articles Leadership · Transformation A title does not make you a leader Vikram Mekala May 2026 · 3 min read But somewhere along the way, organisations forgot that. The loudest voice gets promoted. The best politician gets the senior role. The person who says the right thing in the right room gets the big job. And then the transformation programme fails. And nobody can explain why. I can. The system selected for the wrong thing.

docs.t: A title does not make you a leader
docs.x: Real leadership in a transformation is specific. Do you take the blame when things go wrong or let it roll downhill? Do you create space for your team to think or close it down? Do you back people when they take a risk, or protect yourself when it does not pay off? Do you actually understand the people you are working with? Different cultures, different contexts, different ways of thinking. That is a learnt skill. Not everyone has it. Not everyone bothers. In 26 years across programmes, projects and product delivery, the answer has been the same. People first. Not technology. Not process. Not the word you just added to your LinkedIn headline.

docs.t: A title does not make you a leader
docs.x: I have seen programmes with perfect technology fail because nobody in the room had the trust of the team. And I have seen underfunded, understaffed deliveries held together by one person who knew how to read a room and back their people at the right moment. That is not soft skills. That is the job. There is a real difference between having the title and having actually delivered it. The organisations that get this right have better outcomes. They also have teams that want to be there. The title comes after. Not before. Vikram Mekala 26 years in enterprise transformation. Day 0 Hypercare Lead on the Magnum/Unilever separation. Now building and available for contracts. mekalav.com

docs.t: The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready
docs.x: Vikram Mekala ← All articles AI · Product The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready Vikram Mekala May 2026 · 5 min read When I started building Miru, I set one simple rule: it must work on WhatsApp. It's not about the technology being impressive. It isn't. But it's an app people already have on their phones, they know how to use it, and it requires no new accounts or tutorials. That is exactly the point. I've spent 26 years watching enterprise software fail. The code usually works fine, but the people it was built for don't use it. They avoid it, or they need days of training just to get anything out of it.

docs.t: The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready
docs.x: The pattern is always the same. You build something capable. You add more features. You make it more powerful. Then you realise your users are still doing their work in Excel or just calling someone on the phone. The technology wasn't wrong. The usability was. When I started building AI tools for non-technical people, I thought about my mum. She is in her sixties, lives in India, and uses WhatsApp all day for family and news. She doesn't download new apps, she doesn't create accounts, and she doesn't read through onboarding flows. If she couldn't use a tool within thirty seconds of first opening it, I knew I had built the wrong thing.

docs.t: The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready
docs.x: I stopped asking, "Is this technically capable?" and started asking, "Would a 60-year-old who isn't interested in technology actually use this?" It sounds obvious, but it isn't. Most AI products are built by technical people for other technical people, followed by a press release about democratising AI. Using WhatsApp as a constraint forces you to be useful immediately. There is no interface to hide behind. You can't mask bad thinking with a beautiful design. The user types something in plain English and they get something useful back, or they don't. If they don't, they won't come back. That constraint is brutal, but it creates real clarity.

docs.t: The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready
docs.x: When I built the fuel price feature in Miru, I didn't build a dashboard with filters and charts. I built a way to send a postcode and get the price. When I built the school communication feature, I didn't build a notification centre. I built a tool that reads school emails and messages you only when something needs your attention. When I built the train times feature, you type your station or use your location to get the next departures. The tech underneath is the same as what the big AI companies are building. The difference is the surface, the part people touch.

docs.t: The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready
docs.x: In design, there is a concept called affordance. It means an object should suggest how it is used. A door handle says pull. A push plate says push. Get that wrong and people feel stupid, blaming themselves instead of the design. WhatsApp has perfect affordance for conversation. You know exactly what to do because you just type. No instructions required. No app store. No version updates.

docs.t: The WhatsApp test: if a 60-year-old can use it, it is ready
docs.x: That is why I build there first. Not as a limitation, but as a design principle. If something works well in a text message, you understand what you are building. You can always expand to a web app or a dashboard later. But if you cannot make it work in plain text first, you probably don't understand the problem well enough yet. The "60-year-old test" isn't really about age. It is about honesty. It forces you to ask: have I made this genuinely easy, or have I just made it powerful? Are real people going to use this, or am I just building something that other people in the AI industry will find impressive? Those are two very different products. I know which one I want to build. Vikram Mekala

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: Agentic commerce sounds like jargon. The idea is simple. You tell an AI what you want. It finds the options, compares them and, if you let it, buys the thing. The shopper is still a person. The one doing the clicking isn't. At Unilever I worked on pricing and early eCommerce data, including Amazon. Back then the fight was over the digital shelf: how your product showed up when a person searched. This is the next shelf. Except the one reading it is an agent. The numbers worth knowing It's already changing how people shop. 68% of US consumers used at least one AI tool while shopping in the past three months, according to ICSC and McKinsey.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: AI shoppers are better customers. In September 2026, visits that came from AI tools to US retail sites converted 90% better than other traffic and brought in 83% more revenue per visit (Adobe). That's a big flip. In March 2025, AI traffic converted 38% worse. It's growing fast. AI traffic to US retail sites is up 1,772% since October 2024. Over last year's holiday season it was up 693%. But it's still small. AI platforms will be about 1.5% of US online retail sales in 2026, around $20.6 billion (EMARKETER). Nearly four times last year, but a long way from taking over.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: The forecasts are huge, and all over the place. McKinsey says AI agents could handle $3 to $5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030. Bain says $300 to $500 billion in the US. Morgan Stanley's base case is around $190 billion. Same idea, different definitions. Read the range, not one number. The bit nobody puts on a slide OpenAI launched Instant Checkout in ChatGPT in September 2025, so you could buy without leaving the chat. By March 2026 it was shutting it down.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: Why? Merchants didn't sign up. Forrester reckons only about 30 Shopify merchants were using it by February. ChatGPT needed live stock, delivery times and shipping costs, and scraping websites wasn't enough. Checkout now goes back to the retailer's own site. So the agent is great at finding and comparing. The buying, the returns and the customer relationship still sit with the shop. For now. What it means for brands This is the part that matters most to me, coming from consumer goods. BCG looked at it last month, and a few numbers stood out.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: People use AI to choose, not yet to buy. Of the people who shop with AI, 96% use it to discover products and 80% to weigh them up. Only 24% use it to actually buy. And just 4% would let an agent complete a purchase on its own. Most brands aren't ready. 59% of consumer goods companies have no meaningful agentic AI capability yet. The risk is real. For one global consumer goods company, BCG reckoned 20% to 30% of online revenue could be at risk as discovery moves to AI search.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: The early movers are seeing results. Brands working on showing up in AI answers are seeing 1% to 5% extra revenue. Those building their own agents and plugging into retailers' agents see 3% to 10%. One personal care brand found shoppers who chat with its AI advisor buy about 25% more often. BCG's point is that showing up in AI answers isn't enough on its own. If that's all you do, you end up as one more option the agent compares on price. Where the money is going The payment companies are getting ready anyway.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: Visa launched Agentic Ready in Europe, starting with the UK, with Barclays, HSBC UK, Nationwide and Revolut testing payments started by AI agents. Mastercard's Agent Pay makes agents register and get verified before they can pay for anyone, and the shopper decides what the agent is allowed to buy. That's the real signal. Banks don't build plumbing for fads. What to do about it If you sell things: - Make your products readable by machines. Clear names, specs, sizes, price, stock and delivery times. If an agent can't read it, you don't exist in the answer. - Keep your checkout. Agents will send you the customer. Make the last step on your own site quick and painless.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: - Track AI traffic on its own. Split it out in your analytics. It behaves differently, and it's growing faster than anything else. - Start with one category. Pick the products people research hardest and fix those listings first. If you're a brand: - Find out what people ask AI about your category. Then check whether you show up in the answers, and track it like you'd track search. - Give agents something to recommend together. A routine, a bundle, a refill. An agent that suggests a basket is worth more than one that picks a single item. - Think about your own agent. An advisor that answers real questions about your products, and teaches you what customers actually want.

docs.t: Writing: Your next customer might be an AI
docs.x: - Start with one or two pilots with a retailer or platform, learn, then scale. If you're the shopper: - Let AI do the research and comparing. That's what it's good at today. - If you let it pay, set limits: a spending cap, approved shops, a confirmation step. - Check the returns policy before you buy. The agent won't be the one standing in the queue. If you work in a big company: - Ask who owns this. It sits between eCommerce, marketing, IT and payments, so it's easy for it to belong to nobody. The shop window is moving into the chat. The till isn't. Not yet. ---

docs.t: Writing: AI won't make you an entrepreneur. It'll make you a builder.
docs.x: Everyone keeps saying AI will turn us all into entrepreneurs. I don't buy it. I think it'll turn a lot of us into builders, which isn't the same thing. Building has got cheap A few years ago a small business needed a developer, a designer, someone on support and someone doing ads. Now one person with a laptop and a few AI tools can do most of that over a weekend.

docs.t: Writing: AI won't make you an entrepreneur. It'll make you a builder.
docs.x: I've done it myself. Since last November I've built four AI products on my own, mostly with Claude Code. One of them, Miru, is a WhatsApp assistant that helps with everyday UK stuff like train times, fuel prices and sorting school messages. Building it was the easy bit. Getting 20 people to sign up took a couple of months, and getting someone to pay is still the bit I'm working on. And I'm clearly not the only one. By last year, over a third of new US startups had a single founder, up from under a quarter in 2019, according to Carta's Solo Founders Report. Finding customers hasn't

docs.t: Writing: AI won't make you an entrepreneur. It'll make you a builder.
docs.x: So building isn't really the hard part anymore. Getting people to pay for what you've built is, and then doing it again and again. That's sales and marketing. Most of us would rather avoid it, and AI hasn't changed that much. The App Store shows it well. Around 560,000 new apps went live in the first half of this year, almost as many as in the whole of 2025, but downloads only went up 2% (Sensor Tower data via 9to5Mac). Loads more apps chasing the same people. One developer the New York Times spoke to got 1,300 downloads and made about $500 from it. If you can build something in a week, so can fifty other people.

docs.t: Writing: AI won't make you an entrepreneur. It'll make you a builder.
docs.x: People also say we're just going back to how things used to be, when most people worked for themselves. That's true, but a lot of them didn't have much choice, and plenty were pushed out by bigger players. The 9 to 5 isn't the safe option either None of this means the 9 to 5 is the safe option. It feels safe because the salary turns up every month and someone else worries about finding customers.

docs.t: Writing: AI won't make you an entrepreneur. It'll make you a builder.
docs.x: But in the first five months of this year, US employers blamed AI for nearly 88,000 job cuts, more than 2024 and 2025 combined (Challenger, Gray & Christmas, via Outlook Business). Those are the reasons companies gave, and some of them may be using AI as cover for cuts they'd have made anyway. Either way, a job can go with one email. Both paths carry risk. It just shows up differently. Two questions before you go solo If you're thinking of going it alone, I'd worry less about whether you can build it and more about these two: 1. Who already trusts you enough to buy from you? 2. What do you know about the problem that a stranger with the same tools doesn't?

docs.t: Writing: AI won't make you an entrepreneur. It'll make you a builder.
docs.x: These aren't only questions for founders. Most of us in jobs have never had to find our own customer, because the company does that for us. They're worth asking even if you never leave. If you've got good answers to those, there's never been a better time. If you haven't, a steady job is still a perfectly sensible choice. Just don't assume it's guaranteed. --- I'm building small AI products under Human Agency. More of my work is at mekalav.com.

docs.t: Writing: What actually brings the spark back
docs.x: I saw a post on Threads the other day. Someone asked, "People who finally found their spark back, what genuinely helped?" It's a simple question but it stuck with me. Mostly because the answers weren't what I expected. Nobody said they found their passion or quit everything and moved to Bali. What people actually described was much smaller than that. It came back in small pieces When you read enough of these answers, a pattern shows up. The spark doesn't come back in one go. It comes back in bits, and usually in a certain order.

docs.t: Writing: What actually brings the spark back
docs.x: Rest, but the real kind. A lot of what feels like lost spark is just being tired. Not sleepy tired, empty tired. And scrolling doesn't fix that. It numbs it. Sleep, walks, time with nothing coming in, that's what actually refills the tank. Moving before feeling like it. Cooking, walking, the gym, gardening. People kept saying they didn't wait to feel motivated. They moved first and the motivation followed. It's the opposite of how we usually think it works. Making something for no reason. A sketch, a bit of writing, a small app nobody asked for. No audience, no plan to sell it. Play seems to bring the spark back faster than goals do.

docs.t: Writing: What actually brings the spark back
docs.x: Being around people who light up. Energy rubs off. One good conversation with someone who's excited about what they do can do more than weeks of thinking about it on your own. Following small curiosities. Not "what's my purpose" but "what am I a bit interested in today?" Then actually following it for an hour. Big questions tend to freeze people. Small ones get them moving. The one that stuck with me One idea kept coming up in different words. People lost their spark when everything started to feel like it had to count.

docs.t: Writing: What actually brings the spark back
docs.x: Every project had to be a proof point. Every hobby had to become a side hustle. Every coffee was networking. Every week was measured against where they thought they should be by now. When everything carries that much weight, nothing feels light anymore. And it's hard to feel a spark about something that feels heavy. What helped wasn't lowering the stakes on everything. It was letting one thing off the hook. One thing that didn't need to lead anywhere. Funnily enough, that's often where the spark came back first, and then it spread. Notice what's taking it The last thing people mentioned was quieter. Sometimes the spark doesn't need finding. It just needs to stop leaking out.

docs.t: Writing: What actually brings the spark back
docs.x: A job that doesn't fit anymore. A person who always leaves you a bit flatter. A story you keep telling yourself about where you should be. Once people noticed what was draining them and stopped feeding it, the spark often came back on its own. I don't think there's a formula here. But if you're in a flat patch right now, maybe start small. Rest properly. Make something for fun. Talk to someone who's excited about something. Let one thing not matter. And if you've been through this and found your way back, I'd genuinely like to know what helped you.

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: I went to The Fifth Day, a workshop by The Do Lectures, on Friday 23 October. It was my first Do Lectures event. I've followed them for years, so I was really looking forward to it. It was at Cecil Sharp House in Camden Town, such a lovely part of London. It rained all day, but I didn't mind. I was excited from the moment I got there.

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: The morning of the event, David and Gemma sent a prompt pack and a short list of what to bring: our own AI tool, mobile data in case the wifi was slow, and ideally our email connected so the AI could look through invoices and receipts. If you didn't want to do that, you could use a bank statement with the personal details taken out, or some dummy data they'd prepared. I liked that they thought about privacy and about people who weren't set up.

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: The day was about using AI to find where a small business quietly loses time and money. The prompts had names like Subscription Audit, Profit Detective, The Invisible Leak and The 5% Detective. Each one sends the AI off to look for something specific, and then you look at what it found. The question we kept coming back to was: > What is my 5%? It was an interactive workshop, so you could ask a question while David was speaking, not just at the end. It felt like a conversation, not a lecture. And there was always something to eat or drink: breakfast, cookies, coffee, lunch. Nobody had to wonder what was next. What I took away

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: I use AI every day, so I knew a lot of the tools already. What I enjoyed was seeing them used on real money problems, with a whole room trying things at the same time. These are the things I wrote down: - Do not try to do everything. Find your 5%. - There are visible leaks and invisible ones, in money and in time. There's also the cost of underperformance, so it's worth asking what an underperformer really costs you. - Use AI for detection. One idea I liked was taking a screenshot of your home page and asking it what's going wrong. - Does your AI agent know what you actually do? What is it, and who is it for? If you can't say that clearly, it can't help.

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: - Be clear about your outputs, and keep only what's necessary. - Old gold is the new gold. Look back at the old things you've already made and bring them back. - There are no good ideas when you're busy. Do the chores, go outside, and let the ideas come. A few apps were mentioned that I want to look at again: Riverside for podcasts, Loom for screen recording, ElevenLabs for voice, Zapier for automation, Runway, Scrivener, and Shopify Sidekick.

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: For me, the key thing was the structure. Seeing how each prompt is set up, what you ask the AI to look for and how you read what comes back, is something I'll reuse in my own work. The time leaks and the 5% idea are the other half. I want to find my own leaks and put my effort into the 5% that matters most. The people The best part was the people. I made new friends and had some lovely conversations. It was all kinds of people, at very different stages of life and business. Where I could, I used my AI experience and helped a few people with their questions. I really enjoyed that.

docs.t: Writing: The Fifth Day
docs.x: It was great to finally meet David Hieatt. I've followed his journey since the Hiut Denim days, and he's thoughtful and generous. He's got an incredible team too. I met Gemma Screen for the first time, and I saw Ian Laming from Do Radio again. We'd last met a couple of weeks ago at the Poetry Pharmacy, the poetry-on-prescription shop run by Deborah Alma, at the launch of Anna McCracken's new book, Do Wildness: Myth, mystery and mischief. It's published by Do Book Co. and sets out ten practices for reconnecting with the natural world. Anna is an Australian writer, wilderness guide and systems thinker.

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: Most companies don't fail their customers on purpose. They fail them because rigid process and automation stop good people from acting like humans. At a glance {.facts} - Author: John Sills - Publisher: Bloomsbury Business, April 2023 - Recognition: Leadership Book of the Year 2023, Institute of Leadership - ISBN: 9781399401739 - Get it: Find it on Bookshop.org - Read: October 2026 - My verdict: One of the best books I've read on customer experience. I keep going back to it. The big idea Sills makes three points that stuck with me: - The emotional side of an experience matters as much as the functional side. How it felt counts as much as whether it worked.

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: - Getting the human side right doesn't cost more. It makes a business more efficient. - Experience isn't the front line's job alone. Everyone in the organisation shapes it. What I liked most is that he doesn't hand you a checklist. He says each company has to choose the experience that fits its own customers and its own strengths. The framework in one picture Sills sums the book up in seven behaviours customers can feel, held up by five enablers inside the organisation. The behaviours are what customers notice. The enablers are what lets your people behave that way without fighting the system. Stories that stayed with me

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: The book is full of real examples, mostly from UK companies. These are the ones I keep thinking about. Octopus Energy and the battery pack. Engineers brought a battery pack when fitting smart meters, so the customer's Wi-Fi stayed on. Small thing. But someone was thinking about the customer, not just the job. Octopus and "put Harry on the phone". When Octopus was small, a customer with a problem got the person who knew them. At around 50,000 customers they split into specialist teams and lost that. So they rebuilt teams to own a customer from start to finish, with no scripts.

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: AO.com and the anniversary plant. A driver called ahead before delivering a fridge. The customer's son mentioned it was his parents' wedding anniversary. The driver stopped, bought a pot plant in AO colours and handed it over at the door. No process asks for that. AO just trusts its people to treat customers like their own gran. NHS Blood and Transplant. Complaints are owned by whoever was involved, not passed to a generic team. And donors get thank-you dinners, which they describe as recognition, not reward. Chiltern Railways. Senior managers travel on their own trains, name badge on. Every new starter is told their one job is to make the right decisions for customers.

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: Citymapper. Simple "Report Issue" and "Get Me Home" buttons. The app takes responsibility for getting you where you need to be. Lines worth remembering - "Treat every customer as if they were your own gran." AO.com - "If companies treat people like adults, they'll respond like adults." NHS Blood and Transplant - "Human relationships shouldn't be defined by a training manual." Riverford - People are only consumers for a few hours of the day. Stan Sthanunathan, from his Unilever days - Making staff escalate for permission is "handcuffing them". Workday

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: One more thing that surprised me: most executives think they deliver great customer experience, but only about one in three customers feel their favourite brands really understand them. What I'm taking from it I read it as a delivery person, and it fits programmes just as well as customer service. - Telling the business what will break before they find out is the programme version of the battery pack. - The drop from a great pitch team to the delivery team is the same as Octopus losing "Harry". - Stakeholders are only stakeholders for a few hours a day. The rest of the time our programme is getting in the way of their real job.

docs.t: Writing: The Human Experience
docs.x: It also shapes how I think about AI. Most AI work is about automating steps. This book is a good reminder that the point is to free people up to act like humans, not to script them further. Who should read it: anyone who leads teams, runs a service or delivers change. It's full of real stories and it's genuinely warm.

docs.t: Writing: The jobs stayed. The pay didn't.
docs.x: Most of the talk about AI and jobs is about jobs disappearing. I think there's a quieter story that matters more. The job stays. It just stops mattering who does it. Economists Masao Fukui, Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson have a name for this: the commoditisation of labour. Their paper is about something older than AI, but it explains a lot about where AI might take us. Automation and commoditisation aren't the same thing Automation means a machine takes over the work, so there are fewer jobs.

docs.t: Writing: The jobs stayed. The pay didn't.
docs.x: Commoditisation is different. The work still needs people, but it gets simplified and standardised until almost anyone can do it. Firms stop being picky about who they hire, and people become easy to replace. There are plenty of jobs, but the pay is lower. We've seen this before McDonald's scripted almost every step in the kitchen. Warehouse staff follow instructions from a headset, and training dropped from weeks to days. Call centre staff read answers off a screen. Nobody in those jobs was automated out. They just became interchangeable. The pay followed. In the 1980s, the biggest US employers paid almost 60% more than small firms. By the 2010s it was about 20%. I know this from the inside

docs.t: Writing: The jobs stayed. The pay didn't.
docs.x: At BP I ran a six-month transition handing people, processes and systems over to an incoming vendor. The whole job was making sure the work no longer depended on who was doing it. AI does the same thing, only faster. Developers review generated code instead of writing it. Service desks pick from suggested answers. PMs get status reports drafted for them. More people can do the work, so firms get less picky about who they hire. The documents are the easy part Anyone who's run a transition knows the hard part is what never got written down. Things like: - knowing who needs a heads-up before a change goes live - knowing which "known issue" you can ignore and which one you can't

docs.t: Writing: The jobs stayed. The pay didn't.
docs.x: - knowing why that old workaround is still there, and what breaks if you take it out That know-how is what keeps a person hard to replace. It's also what gets lost when a role is standardised without much thought. If you lead an enterprise IT team - Before you standardise a role with AI, ask what you'd lose if that person left tomorrow. Protect that. - Don't judge AI rollouts on cost per head alone. Track rework, incidents and decisions that had to be reversed. - Bring the people who know the unwritten stuff into the rollout early. Don't just ask them to test it at the end. If you work in one

docs.t: Writing: The jobs stayed. The pay didn't.
docs.x: - Stop asking "will AI replace me?" Ask which part of your work still needs you specifically, and do more of it. - Spend more time where decisions get made, not just where the work gets done. If AI makes the doing easy, what's left to get paid for is judgment. --- The paper: The Commoditization of Labor, Fukui, Nakamura and Steinsson (2026).
